etymology: From the Greek drachme through the Latin drachma and Old French drame, a small weight and the coin struck to it; the Authorized Version uses dram to render the Hebrew darkemon and adarkon, the Persian daric of gold.
biblical_def: A dram is a small gold coin of the Persian empire, weighed rather than counted, which the Authorized Version sets in the returning-exile books and in David’s last assembly. It is a word of the treasury, and every time it appears it appears in a list of what men gave willingly toward the house of God. David, having set the pattern with his own substance, records what the princes offered for the temple his son would build: gold, and silver, and brass, and iron, and among them “ten thousand drams” (1Ch 29:7). Ezra records the same generosity on the far side of the captivity, when a poor and diminished people gave “after their ability” threescore and one thousand drams of gold to the work (Ezr 2:69), and Nehemiah numbers the Tirshatha’s thousand and the fathers’ twenty thousand (Neh 7:70–72). Small coins, told in heaps, given by many hands. The doctrine of the dram is the doctrine David spoke over the heap: that we are able to offer willingly only because all things come of God, and that what we lay down is of His own already given us (1Ch 29:14). The dram therefore never establishes a claim upon God. It is a returning, not a purchase; a confession that the Giver owns the gift and the giver both, and that the house of God is built by grace flowing back to its source.
webster_summary: A small weight and coin; in Scripture the Persian gold daric, reckoned by tens of thousands among the freewill offerings for the house of God.
webster_full: DRAM, n. [Gr. drachme; L. drachma.] Among the ancients, a small weight and a silver coin.
In apothecaries’ weight, the eighth part of an ounce; in avoirdupois, the sixteenth part.
In the Scriptures, a coin of gold, the Persian daric, rendered dram in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah.
Hence, any small quantity; a little; as much as one may drink at once.
The word marks the smallness of the single piece against the greatness of the sum gathered.
scriptures: And gave for the service of the house of God of gold five thousand talents and ten thousand drams, and of silver ten thousand talents, and of brass eighteen thousand talents, and one hundred thousand talents of iron.
Ezr 2:69
They gave after their ability unto the treasure of the work threescore and one thousand drams of gold, and five thousand pound of silver, and one hundred priests' garments.
Neh 7:70
And some of the chief of the fathers gave unto the work. The Tirshatha gave to the treasure a thousand drams of gold, fifty basons, five hundred and thirty priests' garments.
Neh 7:72
And that which the rest of the people gave was twenty thousand drams of gold, and two thousand pound of silver, and threescore and seven priests' garments.
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel takes the drams laid down for the house of God and turns them into seed money — a transaction with heaven rather than a returning of what heaven gave.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the prosperity gospel, which has made the offering plate a place of exchange. Its preachers — the name-it-and-claim-it line running from Kenyon and Hagin down to the television ministries of our own day — teach that money given is money sown, and that God is bound by a law of return to multiply it back to the giver in kind. Paul named that error before it had its modern name, warning of men “supposing that gain is godliness” (1Ti 6:5), and adding that the love of money is the root of all evil, which some coveting have erred from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. The dram texts destroy the scheme at its foundation. David’s princes did not give in order to receive; they gave because they had already received, and David’s doxology over the heap confessed that all things come of God and that of His own they had given Him. Where giving is a lever upon God it has ceased to be worship and become commerce, and the poor are the ones bled by it.

Recover the willingness and the smallness. Ezra’s returned remnant gave “after their ability” — the measure is not the sum but the ability, which is why the widow’s two mites outweighed the rich men’s abundance in the Lord’s own reckoning. A dram is a small coin; sixty-one thousand of them are a temple treasury. The church is not built by a few great patrons but by many ordinary hands laying down small things cheerfully, and the God who owns the gold of every hill is pleased to receive from His people what was already His. Give as a debtor to grace, not as a creditor to God.
roots_summary: The Persian gold daric; the small coin whose heaps built the house of God out of freely given substance.
roots_lines: Dram — Greek drachme, Latin drachma, Old French drame: a weight and the coin struck to it.
Hebrew darkemon / adarkon, the Persian daric of gold (Ezr 2:69; Neh 7:70–72; 1Ch 29:7).
Every biblical occurrence stands in a list of gifts toward the temple or its rebuilding.
Distinguished from the talent, a great weight; the dram is the small piece.
David’s rule over the whole heap: of thine own have we given thee (1Ch 29:14).
usage: Drams are counted in tens of thousands: the sum is large because the givers were many, not because each was rich.
Read every dram text with David’s confession attached — the gift returns to its Owner.
Ezra’s “after their ability” is the standard by which giving is measured, not the printed total.

etymology: From the Old French boissel, a small box or measure, through Low Latin bustellus; in the Authorized Version it renders the Greek modios, the dry measure of about a peck, and by extension the vessel that held it.
biblical_def: A bushel is a dry measure and the vessel that contains it — a common household tub, wide enough and deep enough to cover a burning lamp and put out its light. Our Lord uses it three times, and always in the same argument: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house” (Mat 5:15). The point is not the measure but the absurdity. No man kindles a flame in order to hide it; the very act of lighting declares an intention that it be seen. Mark adds a second hiding place, the bed, and puts the whole in the form of a question the disciples must answer for themselves (Mar 4:21); Luke adds the secret place and names the purpose plainly, “that they which come in may see the light” (Luk 11:33). The candle is not the believer’s own light. Christ is the light of the world (Joh 8:12), and the church shines only as the moon shines. But the borrowed light is real light, and it was given for a house full of people. Therefore the visibility of the church is not vanity but obedience: let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven (Mat 5:16). A hidden Christian is a contradiction of the purpose for which he was lit.
webster_summary: A dry measure of eight gallons, and the vessel holding it; in the Gospels the covering under which no man puts a lighted candle.
webster_full: BUSHEL, n. [Old French boissel; Low Latin bustellus, a little box.] A dry measure containing eight gallons or four pecks.
Also, the vessel or tub in which that quantity is measured.
In the New Testament it renders the Greek modios, a measure of about a peck.
Figuratively, whatever conceals or smothers what was meant to be seen.
To hide one’s light under a bushel is proverbial in English from Matthew 5:15.
scriptures: Mat 5:15
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Mar 4:21
And he said unto them, Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick?
No man, when he hath lighted a candle, putteth it in a secret place, neither under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that they which come in may see the light.
Mat 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
corruption_summary: The saying is bent into a self-esteem slogan about unused talent, and, at the other extreme, into a warrant for a church that hides its doctrine to keep the world’s goodwill.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite misuses run at once. The first empties the text of God: “don’t hide your light under a bushel” is quoted at graduations and in motivational speech to mean that a man should display his gifts and not be modest about them. That is the exact reverse of the sentence following, which orders the light shown so that men glorify the Father and not the lamp. The second misuse is quieter and does more damage in the churches: a ministry that trims what it confesses, keeps its doctrine off its website, and speaks of sin only in words the world cannot take offence at — and calls this wisdom. It is the bushel, however carefully carpentered. The Lord did not say the candle should be set where none may stumble over it; He said it should be set where all in the house may see it. A church ashamed of the whole counsel of God has not become winsome; it has gone out.

Recover the purpose clause. The candle is lit for the house, and the house is full of people who came in out of the dark. What must be seen is good works — a life ordered by God’s law, a marriage kept, a word kept, wages paid, the poor cared for — and the doctrine that produced them, so that the glory lands where it belongs. Visibility is not self-promotion when the light is borrowed and the praise is redirected. Take the tub off. Let the neighbours know what you believe and see how you live, and leave the glorifying to God.
roots_summary: A dry measure and its tub; the Gospel figure for anything that smothers the light Christ kindled to be seen.
roots_lines: Bushel — Old French boissel, a little box; Low Latin bustellus.
Greek modios, a dry measure of about a peck and the vessel that held it.
Three Gospel occurrences, all of the same saying: Mat 5:15; Mar 4:21; Luk 11:33.
Paired always with the candlestick — the wrong place against the right one.
Mark adds the bed, Luke the secret place: the ways of hiding are many, the lamp is one.
usage: The saying is about the church’s witness, not about a man’s unused abilities.
Mat 5:16 supplies the purpose: that they may glorify your Father, not admire you.
A doctrine kept quiet for the sake of reputation is a bushel by another name.

etymology: From land joined to mark, the Saxon mearc, a boundary or sign; in the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew gebul, the border or bound of a man’s inheritance, commonly a set stone.
biblical_def: A landmark is the stone or heap set in the ground to mark where one man’s inheritance ends and his neighbour’s begins. In Israel these bounds were not invented by surveyors but assigned by lot under God’s hand when Canaan was divided, and the family that held a field held it from the LORD, who said the land is Mine (Lev 25:23). To move the stone by night, therefore, was not a small trespass upon a neighbour but a quiet theft of what God Himself had apportioned, and the law treats it so: “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour’s landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance” (Deu 19:14). It is among the twelve curses pronounced from mount Ebal — “Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour’s landmark” (Deu 27:17) — and the whole congregation answered Amen to it, because the crime is done in secret and only God can be its witness. Solomon repeats the charge twice, adding what makes the sin foulest: “Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless” (Pro 23:10), for their Redeemer is mighty and will plead their cause. Job numbers landmark-removers among the works of darkness (Job 24:2). The stone stands for every settled bound God has set — in property, in the family, in the doctrine once delivered to the saints — and the thief is always the man who profits by moving it a little at a time.
webster_summary: A mark or fixed object — commonly a stone — designating the boundary of a man’s land; its removal is forbidden by the eighth commandment and cursed at Ebal.
webster_full: LANDMARK, n. A mark to designate the boundary of land; any mark or fixed object, as a stone, ditch, tree, or heap, by which the limits of a farm or estate are known.
From land and mark, Saxon mearc, a bound or sign.
Hebrew gebul, a border; the bound of an inheritance divided by lot.
To remove a landmark is a species of theft, prohibited Deu 19:14 and cursed Deu 27:17.
Figuratively, any long-settled principle or bound which men attempt to shift.
scriptures: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance, which thou shalt inherit in the land that the LORD thy God giveth thee to possess it.
Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark. And all the people shall say, Amen.
Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless:
corruption_summary: The removal of ancient bounds is now called progress: the marks God set in creation and in the confessions are shifted a little at a time, and the man who points at the old stone is called the offender.
corruption_paragraphs: Begin with the plain sense, because it is under attack too. The landmark texts assume private property held under God and defended by His law — the eighth commandment gives a man a field the state and his neighbour may not quietly annex. Any scheme, ancient or modern, that treats property as merely a social allotment to be redrawn by whoever holds power is standing exactly where the night-time stone-mover stood. But the figure reaches further, as Scripture’s own use of borders and bounds reaches further. God set bounds in creation: two sexes, male and female, made in His image (Gen 1:27); marriage as one man and one woman for life (Gen 2:24; Mat 19:4–6); the ordered headship of husband and wife and the eldership of qualified men in the church (Eph 5:22–33; 1Ti 2:12–13). These are landmarks, set by the Father of lights and not by custom, and the great work of our age has been to move them by inches while insisting nothing has moved. The same hand moves doctrinal stones: a confession quietly dropped, an article reinterpreted, a word left in place with its meaning drawn out of it.

Recover the two halves of the command. First, honour the bound that belongs to your neighbour — deal honestly in land and in trade, pay what you owe, do not enlarge yourself at the expense of the fatherless, whose Redeemer is mighty. Second, do not be the generation that removes what your fathers set. This is not veneration of the past for its own sake; Scripture requires that a bound be examined by the Word, and where the fathers set a stone the Word did not authorise, it must go. But the ancient landmark is by definition the one set by them of old time under God’s hand, and the burden of proof lies wholly upon the man with the crowbar. Move nothing you cannot show God moved first.
roots_summary: The boundary stone of an inheritance divided by lot; the eighth commandment’s guard upon property and, by figure, upon every settled bound God has set.
roots_lines: Landmark — land + Saxon mearc, a bound, mark or sign.
Hebrew gebul, border; the marked limit of a family inheritance (Deu 19:14).
Cursed at Ebal because the crime is secret and God alone the witness (Deu 27:17).
Solomon twice forbids it, joining it to the fields of the fatherless (Pro 22:28; 23:10).
Job lists it among the deeds of those who rebel against the light (Job 24:2).
usage: The command is an application of the eighth commandment: the stone protects a title God gave.
“Ancient” means set by them of old time under God’s hand — not merely old.
The fatherless clause tells you who is usually robbed: the one with no man to plead for him.

etymology: From the Latin creditor, one who trusts or lends, from credere, to believe or entrust; in Scripture the man to whom a debt is owed, holding a claim upon the debtor’s goods, land, and even his person.
biblical_def: A creditor is one who has lent and to whom repayment is owed. Scripture neither forbids lending nor treats the creditor’s claim as unjust; it hedges his claim about with mercy. Every seventh year the release was proclaimed: “Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD’S release” (Deu 15:2). The debt was real, and the remission was real, and the ground of the remission was the character of God, not the poverty of the borrower. Where that law was neglected the creditor’s power became terrible, as in the prophet’s widow who cried to Elisha that “the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen” (2Ki 4:1) — and God answered her not by cancelling the debt but by multiplying oil until she could pay it and live on the rest. Solomon states the plain sociology: “the borrower is servant to the lender” (Pro 22:7). Our Lord takes the whole figure into the doctrine of forgiveness. To Simon the Pharisee He set two debtors of one creditor, five hundred pence and fifty, neither able to pay, both frankly forgiven, and asked which would love him most (Luk 7:41–42). Simon judged rightly, and condemned himself in judging: the woman washing Christ’s feet with tears knew the size of her debt. Little love is the mark, not of little sin, but of little sense of it.
webster_summary: One to whom a debt is due; in Scripture a lawful office bounded by the seventh-year release, and Christ’s figure for the God who frankly forgives.
webster_full: CREDITOR, n. [L. creditor, from credere, to trust.] A person to whom a sum of money or other thing is due, by obligation, promise or in law.
Opposed to debtor; in book-keeping, the side on which payments received are entered.
In the Mosaic law the creditor’s claim was released in the seventh year (Deu 15:2).
He might not take the widow’s raiment nor the millstone to pledge (Deu 24:6, 17).
Figuratively, one who has a just claim of any kind upon another.
scriptures: Deu 15:2

And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD'S release.

Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets unto Elisha, saying, Thy servant my husband is dead; and thou knowest that thy servant did fear the LORD: and the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen.
Luk 7:41
There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty.
Luk 7:42
And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?
corruption_summary: The parable of the two debtors is preached as an encouragement to forgive ourselves and one another, with the creditor’s real claim and the reason for the greater love quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the softening of the debt. Modern preaching often treats forgiveness as the release of a grudge — something the offended party does for his own peace — and reads Luk 7 as a lesson in generosity of spirit. But the parable turns on a sum that was genuinely owed and genuinely unpayable: “when they had nothing to pay.” God does not forgive by pretending the account is small; He forgives by having the account settled in the blood of His Son, so that the remission is both free to us and costly to Him. Strip the debt of its reality and the woman’s tears become sentiment, Simon’s coldness becomes a personality trait, and the gospel becomes God’s decision to overlook. The other error runs the opposite way: a creditor’s religion which presses the last farthing from a brother while pleading grace for itself — the unmerciful servant of Mat 18, forgiven ten thousand talents and taking his fellow by the throat for a hundred pence.

Recover the arithmetic of love. He to whom much is forgiven loveth much; and the man who thinks his own debt was fifty pence will love little and serve coldly, however orthodox his profession. Recover also the seventh-year mercy in its own sphere. The release was not the abolition of lending but the refusal to let a brother be ground permanently into bondage by his obligations — the same instinct that would not take a widow’s garment in pledge. Lend honestly, keep your word, pay what you owe; and when you hold a claim over a brother whom God has already forgiven ten thousand talents, remember whose release it is called.
roots_summary: One to whom a debt is due; hedged by the LORD’S release, and made by Christ the picture of the God who forgives what could never be paid.
roots_lines: Creditor — Latin creditor, from credere, to trust or entrust.
Hebrew nashah / baal mashsheh yad, the master of the loan of the hand (Deu 15:2).
Greek daneistes, the money-lender of the parable (Luk 7:41).
The seventh-year release is called the LORD’S, not the borrower’s (Deu 15:2).
Elisha’s widow: the creditor’s lawful claim answered by God’s provision, not by default.
usage: Scripture regulates the creditor; it does not abolish lending or excuse the debtor.
The two-debtor parable measures love by the sense of the debt forgiven, not by temperament.
“Nothing to pay” is the state of every sinner before God — the only qualification for free remission.

etymology: From the French lever, to raise, through the Latin levare, to lift; hence a raising — of men for labour or war, or of money or goods as a tribute. The Authorized Version uses it chiefly of Solomon’s conscripted labour and of the tribute raised unto the LORD from the spoil.
biblical_def: A levy is a raising — of men, of goods, or of money — exacted by authority. Scripture uses the word in two very different keys. The first is holy: after the war with Midian the LORD commands, “levy a tribute unto the LORD of the men of war which went out to battle: one soul of five hundred” (Num 31:28), with a heavier portion of fifty from the congregation’s half given to the Levites (Num 31:30). Here the levy confesses that the victory and the spoil were God’s before they were Israel’s, and that the first fruit of every increase belongs to Him. The second key is grave. “King Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel; and the levy was thirty thousand men” (1Ki 5:13), sent by courses to Lebanon under Adoniram, and the chronicler explains its purpose: to build the house of the LORD, and Solomon’s own house, and Millo, and the walls of Jerusalem and the fortified cities (1Ki 9:15). The temple was built by it; so was the king’s magnificence. Samuel had warned exactly this when Israel demanded a king like the nations: he will take your sons, and your fields, and your vineyards, and ye shall cry out in that day (1Sa 8:11–18). The reckoning came at Shechem, when Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute, and all Israel stoned him (1Ki 12:18), and the kingdom tore in two. A levy for God is worship; a levy that consumes the people for a king’s glory ends in stones.
webster_summary: A raising or collecting — of troops, forced labourers, or tribute; in Scripture both the holy portion levied unto the LORD and Solomon’s conscription that broke the kingdom.
webster_full: LEVY, n. [French lever, to raise; L. levare.] The act of raising men for military service; troops so raised.
The act of collecting money by authority; a tax, tribute, or exaction so raised.
In the Scriptures, the body of men raised by Solomon for forced labour (1Ki 5:13; 9:15).
To levy war, to raise or begin war; to take arms for attack.
To levy a tribute unto the LORD, to set apart His portion out of the spoil (Num 31:28).
scriptures: And king Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel; and the levy was thirty thousand men.
And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the LORD, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer.
And levy a tribute unto the LORD of the men of war which went out to battle: one soul of five hundred, both of the persons, and of the beeves, and of the asses, and of the sheep:
And he will take your fields, and your vineyards, and your oliveyards, even the best of them, and give them to his servants.
corruption_summary: Solomon’s levy is read as mere administrative history, and Samuel’s warning about what kings take is quietly detached from the state that takes far more today.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is not a modern redefinition of the word but a modern deafness to the text. Samuel’s speech in 1Sa 8 is a plain prophecy of what centralised power does: it takes sons, daughters, fields, vineyards, oliveyards, servants and a tenth of the increase, and the people who asked for it will cry out and not be heard. The chronicler shows the prophecy fulfilled in Israel’s wisest king, whose levy of thirty thousand built both the temple and Millo, and in his son, whose promise to add to the yoke cost him ten tribes. Scripture treats the family, the church, and the civil magistrate as three distinct authorities under God, each bounded; a levy is lawful within the magistrate’s sphere — render tribute to whom tribute is due (Rom 13:7) — and unlawful when it swallows the other spheres and the man’s inheritance with them. Reading Solomon’s levy as neutral bureaucracy loses the warning God troubled to record twice.

Recover the levy unto the LORD as the pattern of every rightful claim upon a man’s substance. God’s portion out of the Midianite spoil was small — one of five hundred from the soldiers, one of fifty from the congregation — and it was rendered gladly because the whole was His gift. Where a claim is God’s, it is worship; where it is Caesar’s and lawful, it is duty; where it is a king’s appetite dressed as necessity, it is the thing Samuel warned of and Rehoboam learned too late. Give God His portion first, pay the magistrate what is honestly due, and do not confuse the two.
roots_summary: A raising of men or goods by authority; holy when levied unto the LORD, ruinous when a king consumes his people to build his own house.
roots_lines: Levy — French lever, Latin levare, to raise or lift up.
Hebrew mas, a burden or forced-labour gang (1Ki 5:13; 9:15; 12:18).
Adoniram, and after him Adoram, was over the levy — and was stoned for it (1Ki 12:18).
Num 31:28 uses the verb of God’s own portion out of the spoil of Midian.
Samuel’s warning (1Sa 8:11–18) is the interpretive key to Solomon’s levy.
usage: Distinguish the levy unto the LORD from the levy out of Israel — one is worship, the other burden.
The temple and Millo were built by the same gangs; note that Scripture records both purposes together.
Rehoboam’s tribute-officer stoned at Shechem is the historical verdict on an unrelieved yoke.

etymology: From the Old French marchandise, through Latin mercari, to trade, and merx, wares; hence goods bought and sold, and the act of trading in them. Scripture uses both the honest sense and the sense of trafficking in what must never be sold.
biblical_def: Merchandise is goods bought and sold, and by extension the trade itself. Scripture honours it. The virtuous woman of Proverbs 31 is a trader: “She perceiveth that her merchandise is good: her candle goeth not out by night” (Pro 31:18) — she buys a field, plants a vineyard, makes fine linen and delivers girdles to the merchant, and she is praised for it in a chapter which is the Bible’s fullest portrait of an excellent wife. Wisdom herself is commended by the figure: “the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver” (Pro 3:14), which assumes that trade in silver is a real and understood good. Lawful calling in commerce is honest labour under God, and the eighth commandment stands behind every fair sale. But the word turns black in three places. It is forbidden to make merchandise of a person: the captive woman may not be sold (Deu 21:14), and the man-stealer who maketh merchandise of his brother shall die (Deu 24:7). It is forbidden in the house of God: Christ, with a scourge of small cords, drove out the sellers, saying, “make not my Father’s house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16). And it is the last cargo of Babylon, whose merchants weep because no man buyeth their merchandise any more (Rev 18:11), a lading that ends with slaves and the souls of men. Trade is lawful; the traffic in worship and in souls is not.
webster_summary: The wares of trade and the trading itself; honoured as lawful calling, forbidden absolutely in the traffic of souls and in the house of God.
webster_full: MERCHANDISE, n. [French marchandise; L. merx, wares.] The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.
Trade; traffic; commerce; the act of buying and selling.
v. i. To trade; to carry on commerce.
To make merchandise of a person is to traffic in him — forbidden Deu 24:7 on pain of death.
Applied figuratively to wisdom, whose merchandise is better than that of silver (Pro 3:14).
scriptures: She perceiveth that her merchandise is good: her candle goeth not out by night.
Pro 3:14
For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold.
Joh 2:16
And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
Deu 24:7
If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you.
corruption_summary: Worship is packaged and sold as a product, and the flock is made merchandise by men who preach for gain; meanwhile the opposite error despises lawful trade as though commerce were itself unclean.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter warned that false teachers through covetousness would with feigned words make merchandise of the flock (2Pe 2:3), and the warning has never wanted examples. The prosperity ministries sell anointed cloths, miracle water, and seed-faith covenants; the church-growth industry sells worship itself — the service designed as a product, the singing engineered for its effect on the room, the preaching shaped by what the market will bear and the giving campaign built on the same instincts as a sales funnel. Christ’s scourge fell on men doing something far less brazen: selling doves for sacrifice, a genuine convenience for pilgrims, in the outer court of the temple. If that was enough to make His Father’s house an house of merchandise, the trade conducted in His name today is not a lesser thing. Babylon’s manifest ends where such trade always ends — with slaves, and souls of men.

Be evenhanded, for the opposite error is also a corruption. Scripture does not despise commerce. The excellent wife trades and is praised; Lydia sold purple and her house became a church; Paul made tents; private property is guarded by the eighth commandment and the landmark law. A piety that treats business as second-class, or treats profit as theft by definition, has left the Bible for another book. The rule is simply this: sell honestly in the market, with just weights and a kept word, and sell nothing in the sanctuary. Wares are for the market; worship, the ministry of the Word, and the souls of men are not for sale at any price.
roots_summary: The wares and the trading; a lawful calling under God, and an abomination when the goods are worship or men.
roots_lines: Merchandise — Old French marchandise; Latin merx, wares, and mercari, to trade.
Hebrew sachar (to travel about trading) and 'amar (Deu 24:7, to deal tyrannously with).
Greek emporion (Joh 2:16, a place of traffic) and emporeuomai (2Pe 2:3, to make gain of).
Pro 31:18 and Pro 3:14 set the honourable sense; Joh 2:16 and Deu 24:7 the forbidden.
Rev 18:11–13 closes the theme: Babylon’s cargo ends in slaves and souls of men.
usage: The word is morally neutral until you ask what is being sold and where.
Joh 2:16 governs the sanctuary; Pro 31:18 governs the market. Do not swap them.
“Make merchandise of” in Deu 24:7 and 2Pe 2:3 always means trafficking in persons or souls.

etymology: From the Low Latin bursa, a hide or bag, through Old French borse; hence the small pouch, commonly of leather and drawn with a string, in which money was carried. In the Gospels it renders the Greek ballantion and, in the girdle sense, zone.
biblical_def: A purse is the small bag in which a man carried his money. Scripture’s first use of it is an invitation to sin. The enticing sinners of Proverbs 1 say, “Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse” (Pro 1:14) — a promise of common fortune and easy plunder, offered to a young man before he has learned what such fellowship costs; and Solomon’s answer is that they lay wait for their own blood. The common purse is the oldest recruiting argument there is, and its modern forms are no different. Against it stands the Lord’s commission to the seventy: “Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes: and salute no man by the way” (Luk 10:4). This was not a permanent rule of ministry but a deliberate school in dependence, and when He asked them afterward, “lacked ye any thing?” they answered, “Nothing” (Luk 22:35). In the next breath He reverses the instruction for the coming days of hostility — he that hath a purse, let him take it (Luk 22:36) — which shows the first command was for a season and a lesson, not an ordinance of poverty. Haggai supplies the sober counterpoint for a people who put God’s house last: he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes (Hag 1:6). The purse is only a bag. What matters is whose lot is cast in it, and whether the treasure it holds is the kind that faileth not.
webster_summary: A small bag or pouch for money; the figure both of the sinners’ common lot in Proverbs and of the dependence Christ taught by taking it away.
webster_full: PURSE, n. [Low L. bursa, a hide or bag; French bourse.] A small bag in which money is contained or carried, usually made of leather and shut by a string.
Hence, money; the treasury of a state or of a private person; as, the public purse.
A sum of money offered as a prize, or collected as a gift.
In Scripture, the pouch the disciples were forbidden to carry on their first mission (Luk 10:4; Mar 6:8).
To have one purse, to hold goods in common — the enticement of Pro 1:14.
scriptures: Pro 1:14
Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse:
Luk 10:4
Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes: and salute no man by the way.
And he said unto them, When I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing? And they said, Nothing.
Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.
corruption_summary: The empty purse of Luk 10:4 is made a permanent law of ministerial poverty by some and a proof of communal ownership by others, while the enticement of Pro 1:14 is repeated in every scheme that offers a common purse for shared plunder.
corruption_paragraphs: Two abuses of the purse texts are current. The first turns Luk 10:4 into a standing rule — that a true minister must be penniless, that any provision for the man who labours in Word and doctrine is worldliness. Christ Himself dismantles this in Luk 22:36, and Paul settles it: the labourer is worthy of his reward, and they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel (1Ti 5:18; 1Co 9:14). The second abuse presses the same texts, with Act 2:44, into a proof that Christians must hold all things in common as a rule of the kingdom — forgetting Peter’s word to Ananias that the land was his own while it remained, and after it was sold in his own power (Act 5:4), which assumes private ownership and makes the giving free. Meanwhile the oldest use of the purse in Scripture, the sinners’ “let us all have one purse,” keeps its power: every enterprise that recruits by promising a share of what is taken from someone else is quoting Proverbs 1 without knowing it.

Recover the lesson Christ actually taught. He emptied their hands for one journey so that they would know, ever after, that they lacked nothing when they had only Him; and He let them take the purse again when the season changed, so that they would not turn the lesson into a law. Handle money as a steward: earn honestly, give freely, owe no man, and remember Haggai’s bag with holes — wages spent on a life that leaves God’s house last will run out through the seams no matter how much goes in. The only purse that holds is the one Christ names in Luk 12:33: bags which wax not old, where no thief approacheth.
roots_summary: The money-pouch; used for the sinners’ common lot, the disciples’ enforced dependence, and the treasure in heaven that no thief reaches.
roots_lines: Purse — Low Latin bursa, a hide or bag; Old French borse.
Greek ballantion, the money-bag (Luk 10:4; 12:33; 22:35–36).
Hebrew kis, the bag of Pro 1:14, also used of the merchant’s weights (Pro 16:11).
Mar 6:8 forbids money in the purse on the twelve’s mission; Luk 22:36 restores it for a new season.
Hag 1:6 gives the counterfeit: a bag with holes, wages spent on a misordered life.
usage: Luk 10:4 is a lesson for a mission, not a permanent law of ministerial poverty (see Luk 22:36).
Pro 1:14’s “one purse” is an enticement to shared plunder, not a model of Christian fellowship.
The purse that lasts is the one Christ describes: bags which wax not old.

etymology: From the Saxon craet, a carriage or waggon, akin to the Welsh cart; a two-wheeled vehicle drawn by beasts for carrying burdens. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew agalah, the waggon of the field and the road.
biblical_def: A cart is a wheeled waggon drawn by oxen or kine, used for sheaves, for goods, and for the road. Its doctrinal weight in Scripture comes from one thing: the Philistines put the ark of God upon one. Having been plagued for keeping it, their priests and diviners counselled, “make a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke” (1Sa 6:7), and God in mercy let the kine carry it straight to Bethshemesh, for He was pleading His own cause among the heathen who had no law. But Israel had a law. The ark was to be borne upon the shoulders of the Kohathites by staves that were never to be removed (Num 4:15; Exo 25:14–15). When David fetched it up, he copied the Philistine method: “they set the ark of God upon a new cart” (2Sa 6:3), and Uzzah, when the oxen shook it, put forth his hand to steady it, and God smote him there for his error, and there he died by the ark of God (2Sa 6:7). The cart was new, the intention was good, the joy was loud, and a man died. David learned the lesson and stated it plainly before the second attempt: “because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order” (1Ch 15:13). The cart is therefore the standing emblem of worship offered by man’s device instead of God’s prescription — sincere, borrowed from the nations, and fatal.
webster_summary: A two-wheeled waggon for burdens; in Scripture the vehicle on which the ark was carried contrary to God’s command, and thus the emblem of worship by human invention.
webster_full: CART, n. [Saxon craet; Welsh cart.] A carriage with two wheels, fitted to be drawn by one horse or by oxen, and used for the carriage of heavy commodities.
In Scripture, the waggon (Hebrew agalah) used for sheaves, goods, and journeys.
The new cart of 1Sa 6:7 and 2Sa 6:3, upon which the ark of God was set.
Cart rope, a strong rope; figuratively, the cords by which men draw iniquity (Isa 5:18).
Proverbially, to set the cart before the horse: to invert the right order of things.
scriptures: Now therefore make a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke, and tie the kine to the cart, and bring their calves home from them:
And they set the ark of God upon a new cart, and brought it out of the house of Abinadab that was in Gibeah: and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drave the new cart.
And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God.
For because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order.
corruption_summary: The new cart is the perpetual argument of the innovator: that God will bless whatever is offered sincerely, newly built, and popular — against which the regulative principle and Uzzah’s grave stand together.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is old and thoroughly modern at once. It says that in worship, sincerity sanctifies the method; that what God has not commanded He has therefore permitted; that the question to ask of a service is whether it moves people and draws them, not whether He appointed it. Every generation builds a new cart. Rome built one of images, relics, and a sacrifice re-offered; the revivalist built one of the anxious bench and engineered decision; our own age builds one of the produced service, the theatrical set, the drama and the dance, and defends it by results. But the ark was not lacking transport — it was lacking the staves and the shoulders God appointed. Note carefully that the cart was borrowed from Philistia, and that the borrowing was the very thing: Israel took her worship-method from the nations because it looked reverent and worked once. It had worked for the Philistines because God was not dealing with them by covenant law.

Recover the due order. This is the regulative principle of worship stated by David himself in 1Ch 15:13: what the LORD commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to add, however new the timber. Uzzah’s death is not an overreaction to a small mistake; it is God’s public verdict that His prescribed way is not a suggestion, and it is recorded so that we need not learn it as David did. The second procession went right because the Levites bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves, as Moses commanded according to the word of the LORD (1Ch 15:15) — and the joy of that day was greater, not less, for being obedient.
roots_summary: The ox-drawn waggon; God’s ark set upon it by man’s device, and the death of Uzzah as the seal upon the due order of worship.
roots_lines: Cart — Saxon craet, a waggon or carriage for burdens.
Hebrew agalah, the waggon of the field, the road, and the Philistine device (1Sa 6:7).
Contrast Num 4:15 and Exo 25:14–15: the ark borne on staves upon Kohathite shoulders.
2Sa 6:3–7 — the new cart, Uzzah’s hand, and the breach at Perezuzzah.
1Ch 15:13–15 — David names the sin (not the due order) and corrects it.
usage: A “new cart” in Reformed usage means an unprescribed method of worship, however sincere.
God’s forbearance toward the Philistines was not a precedent for Israel — they had the law.
1Ch 15:13 is the clearest Old Testament statement of the regulative principle.

etymology: From olive, Latin oliva, joined to yard, the Saxon geard, an enclosure; hence the walled or hedged plantation of olive trees. It renders the Hebrew zayith in the collective, the olive-ground of a family’s inheritance.
biblical_def: An oliveyard is an enclosed plantation of olive trees — slow-growing, long-lived, and the steadiest wealth a family in Canaan could hold, since the tree gives oil for food, for light, for anointing and for the sanctuary, and gives it for generations. Its doctrinal weight lies in a single clause Joshua repeats to the assembled tribes: “I have given you a land for which ye did not labour, and cities which ye built not, and ye dwell in them; of the vineyards and oliveyards which ye planted not do ye eat” (Jos 24:13). Moses had prepared them for the same mercy and warned of its danger — houses they filled not, wells they digged not, olive trees they planted not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full, beware lest thou forget the LORD (Deu 6:11–12). This is unearned inheritance, covenant grace in the shape of trees planted by other men’s hands, and it is the closest thing in the Old Testament to a parable of justification: a people put in possession of a fruitfulness they did not produce. Two dark uses answer it. Samuel warns that the king they demand will take their oliveyards, even the best of them, and give them to his servants (1Sa 8:14). And Elisha, seeing through Gehazi’s lie about Naaman’s silver, asks the question that exposes the heart: “Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards?” (2Ki 5:26). Grace freely given may be neither stolen by a king nor bargained for by a prophet’s servant.
webster_summary: An enclosed plantation of olive trees; in Scripture the emblem of inheritance received without labour — covenant grace in the form of trees Israel never planted.
webster_full: OLIVEYARD, n. [Olive and yard, Saxon geard, an enclosure.] An enclosure or piece of ground in which olives are cultivated.
The olive yields oil for food, for lamps, for anointing, and for the offerings of the sanctuary.
Being slow of growth and long of life, it represents settled and inherited estate.
Named with vineyards in the lists of what Israel received but did not plant (Jos 24:13; Neh 9:25).
Taken away by kings (1Sa 8:14) and restored by repentant rulers (Neh 5:11).
scriptures: And I have given you a land for which ye did not labour, and cities which ye built not, and ye dwell in them; of the vineyards and oliveyards which ye planted not do ye eat.
Deu 6:11
And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full;

And he said unto him, Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards, and sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and maidservants?
Neh 5:11

Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them.
corruption_summary: Unearned inheritance is read as a lesson in gratitude only, with the doctrine beneath it — that God gives what we did not labour for — softened into the notion that Israel earned Canaan by conquest and obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger is nearer home: the quiet assumption that what we hold, we produced. Joshua’s sentence forbids it in the sharpest possible terms — a land ye laboured not for, cities ye built not, oliveyards ye planted not. Israel did fight, and fought hard; but the fighting did not create the olive trees, and Moses had already told them the reason for the gift was not their righteousness, for they were a stiffnecked people (Deu 9:6). This is the shape of grace, and it is the shape of the believer’s whole estate: a righteousness he did not work out, a peace he did not make, a place at a table he did not set. The man who forgets it will do one of two things — boast, or grasp after more. Deu 6:12 names the danger exactly: when thou shalt have eaten and be full, beware lest thou forget the LORD which brought thee forth.

Recover the gratitude and the guard together. Gehazi is the warning for the ministry: a servant of the prophet who saw free grace given to a Syrian and calculated what he could extract from it — oliveyards and vineyards, sheep and oxen — and carried away Naaman’s leprosy with the silver. Samuel is the warning for the state: what a family received as inheritance, a king will take “even the best of them” and hand to his courtiers, which is why the landmark law and the jubilee stood guard over Israel’s fields. And Nehemiah is the pattern of repentance: restore, this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards. Grace received freely makes a man generous, not acquisitive.
roots_summary: Enclosed olive plantations; the trees Israel did not plant, standing for an inheritance wholly of grace.
roots_lines: Oliveyard — olive (Latin oliva) + yard (Saxon geard, an enclosure).
Hebrew zayith, the olive tree and its ground; oil for food, light, anointing and offering.
Jos 24:13 and Deu 6:11 — the unlaboured inheritance, with its warning against forgetting.
1Sa 8:14 — the king will take your oliveyards, even the best of them.
2Ki 5:26 and Neh 5:11 — grasped after by Gehazi, restored by Nehemiah’s reform.
usage: The clause to press is “which ye planted not” — the whole doctrine sits there.
Olive trees outlive their planters, which is why they figure inheritance rather than harvest.
Gehazi’s oliveyards show grace turned into a commodity by a man close to the prophet.

etymology: From reap, the Saxon ripan, to cut grain, akin to ripe; hence those who cut down the standing corn at harvest. It renders the Hebrew qatsar in the participle and the Greek theristes.
biblical_def: Reapers are the labourers who cut the standing corn and bind it, working under an overseer and followed by the gleaners who gather what falls. Scripture gives us one memorable company of them: Boaz’s men in the barley fields of Bethlehem. Ruth the Moabitess “gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech” (Rut 2:3) — her hap, which is providence speaking in the language of ordinary days. Boaz comes from Bethlehem and greets his workmen, “The LORD be with you,” and they answer, “The LORD bless thee” (Rut 2:4): the field is a place of covenant courtesy, not mere labour. He charges the young men not to touch her, bids her drink of their vessels, and commands them to let handfuls fall on purpose. So the kinsman-redeemer is first met among his reapers, providing for a widow in the ordinary channels of harvest and gleaning-law, before he ever stands at the gate to redeem her. Christ takes the same picture into eternity. Expounding the tares, He says the harvest is the end of the world, “and the reapers are the angels” (Mat 13:39), sent to gather the tares in bundles to burn and the wheat into the barn (Mat 13:30). And James warns those who defraud reapers of their hire that the cries have entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth (Jas 5:4). The men in the field foreshadow the angels at the end; the Lord of the harvest pays and reckons both.
webster_summary: Those who cut down the standing corn at harvest; Boaz’s men among whom Ruth gleaned, and Christ’s figure for the angels at the end of the world.
webster_full: REAPER, n. [From reap, Saxon ripan, to cut grain.] One that cuts grain with a sickle; a harvest labourer.
In Scripture, the workmen of the field, followed by gleaners according to the law of Lev 19:9.
The reapers of Boaz among whom Ruth gathered (Rut 2:3–9).
Their hire was due the same day, and fraud in withholding it cries to God (Jas 5:4; Deu 24:15).
Figuratively, the angels sent forth at the end of the world (Mat 13:39).
scriptures: Rut 2:3
And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech.
Rut 2:4
And, behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said unto the reapers, The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee.
The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.
Jas 5:4

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
corruption_summary: The book of Ruth is read as a romance and the reapers as scenery, while the final harvest of Mat 13 is softened until the reapers gather nobody into the fire.
corruption_paragraphs: Two flattenings are common. The first turns Ruth into a love story with a religious setting, so that Boaz is an admirable man rather than the kinsman-redeemer whose right to redeem must be established at the gate, and the field becomes a picturesque backdrop rather than the working of God’s gleaning-law, which fed the widow and the stranger without alms and without shame. The second empties Mat 13:39. The Lord’s own interpretation of the tares is as plain as language can be: the harvest is the end of the world, the reapers are angels, the tares are bound in bundles and burned, and there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. Annihilationist and universalist readings must dispose of that sentence, and no reading which does so has honoured the One who spoke it. The reapers are sent by the Son of man, and their commission includes a fire.

Recover the two harvests together, for they are one lesson. Boaz in the barley field is Christ in the world — the redeemer who greets his labourers with the LORD be with you, who orders handfuls to fall on purpose for a foreign widow with no claim, and who at last takes her to himself by right of kinship and price paid. The angels at the end are the same Lord’s servants completing the same work: gathering His wheat into the barn. And between them stands James’s warning to every employer — pay the reaper his hire, and pay it today, because the Lord of sabaoth hears what the labourer cannot say to your face.
roots_summary: Harvest labourers; Boaz’s men behind whom Ruth gleaned, and the angels the Son of man sends at the end of the world.
roots_lines: Reaper — from reap, Saxon ripan, to cut grain; akin to ripe.
Hebrew qotserim, the cutters (Rut 2:3–9); Greek theristai (Mat 13:39).
The reapers go first, the gleaners follow — the law’s provision for widow and stranger (Lev 19:9).
Boaz sets a servant over the reapers and charges them for Ruth’s protection (Rut 2:5, 9).
Mat 13:30, 39 — tares bound in bundles, wheat into the barn, by angelic hands.
usage: Ruth’s “hap” is the Bible’s way of showing providence dressed as coincidence.
Boaz among his reapers is the kinsman-redeemer before he is ever called that at the gate.
Mat 13:39 identifies the reapers definitively: the angels, at the end of the world.
